doc.title: Bobby Shew interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 1, 2020

title: Music as a way of life; childhood Sunday radio and Peter and the Wolf
summary: Shew calls jazz his religion and philosophy, recalls his family's 78s and the Sunday classical broadcasts, and hearing Peter and the Wolf as a toddler.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: I was going to say it sounds exactly like something I would say. I get so perturbed sometimes you know, and you know I guess I probably, I don’t mean to be an elitist or anything about this music, but I care more about this music than I could even, you know, with all the dictionaries that I own and everything I don’t think I could come up with the words to express my, the depth of my emotional feelings for this music. It’s not just music to me, it’s something greater than that. It’s religion, it’s philosophy, it’s a way of life, it’s the connection to the full meaning of my life ever since I was, when I found out about improvisation it wasn’t — I always liked music as a kid you know, and my parents, and my grandmother and my mom played the old 78 albums and things like that, it was mostly Guy Lombardo and Wayne King, there was one Harry James 78 there you know. But I had no clue who Harry James was.
Right. You didn’t think of this is like really sweet stuff.

No. No I was just — it was music, they loved music and they played music in the house fairly regularly. I mean one of the big things that I always recalled was on Sunday nights that I remember, as best I remember it, there was a thing called the Bell Telephone Hour I believe. And if I’m not mistaken I think it was the New York Philharmonic or something like that that played. It was a New York symphony orchestra. And my grandmother and my mom, they liked Mario Lanza, the Great Caruso, things like that. They liked the opera kind of thing you know. And so they would listen to classical music on Sunday and we would like, well I was probably no more than a year and a half or something, old, I was

laying on a little blanket in a diaper you know. But we listened to that music, and I had an uncle, Tom, who also loved classical music. So we’d gather around in the living room and listen to this thing every Sunday night. And I just remember laying there and listening. But the first one that hit me like a bong in the head was when they did “Peter and the Wolf.” I was probably maybe about two or two and a half years old when I heard that. And a bassoon could be a duck? I thought wow that is the hippest thing in the world you know. Or whatever. The instruments could become animals. And suddenly there was this whole kind of thing happened in my head, it added meaning to it — it wasn’t just sounds it had visual characteristics, characters and a story line and everything you know. For whatever reason I really, to this very day, I can almost go back to that moment on the floor and remember that. That’s weird.
